profile.address: 165 West Park Loop NW, Huntsville, AL 35806
profile.reading:
Simple Helix operates a purpose built colocation data center at 165 West Park Loop NW in Huntsville, Alabama, near Cummings Research Park, the second largest research and technology park in the United States and a hub for the aerospace, defense, and government contractor tenants clustered around the nearby Redstone Arsenal and NASA Marshall Space Flight Center. Simple Helix itself is a locally owned and operated managed IT and hosting provider that has served the Huntsville market for more than fifteen years, with its web hosting line of business dating to 2007, before expanding into dedicated colocation space.

According to the company's own published facility specifications, the Huntsville data center is built to Tier III design standards with two N plus one redundancy across both its power and cooling plants, meaning utility power, backup generation, and uninterruptible power supply capacity are each rated at 4.5 megawatts, a configuration intended to let the facility withstand the loss of any single power path without disrupting customer equipment. Backup fuel is stored on site in a 16,000 gallon tank system equipped with fuel scrubbers to extend generator runtime during an extended utility outage. The building is sited outside the FEMA 100 year floodplain, a siting choice colocation operators commonly make to limit flood exposure, and Simple Helix states the facility is served by three independent access paths for connectivity and secured behind a K4 rated perimeter fence, a crash rating standard used for vehicle barriers at higher security sites.

The compliance posture Simple Helix advertises for the facility, DFARS 252.204-7012, NIST 800-171A, SOC 2 Type II, and PCI, alongside an in progress push toward CMMC 2.0 certification, tracks closely with the customer base its Huntsville location is positioned to serve, defense contractors and subcontractors working with Redstone Arsenal and the broader Department of Defense footprint in the Tennessee Valley, for whom NIST 800-171 and the eventual Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification requirements are a condition of doing business rather than a marketing choice. That alignment between the facility's stated certifications and the defense industrial concentration of its home market is one of the more informative facts publicly available about the site, even though Simple Helix does not publish its total data hall square footage, its current occupancy or tenant list, or the identity of the general contractor or engineer of record for the build. Those figures, along with the exact year of construction and any expansion history, are not part of the company's public materials as of this writing.

reading.body:
SimpleHelix's Huntsville facility provides 4.5 MW of critical IT capacity with tripled power paths, placing it among small regional data centers oriented toward compliance-heavy workloads rather than hyperscale AI training.

The facility's power architecture reveals its design purpose. Utility power, generator capacity, and UPS capacity all match at 4.5 MW, with 2N plus 1 redundancy across all three. This symmetry is uncommon in larger centers and indicates a facility built for continuous availability to applications that cannot tolerate outages, not for maximum compute density. The 16,000 gallon on-site fuel storage supports multi-day runtime in grid failures.

The compliance footprint is dense relative to capacity. DFARS, NIST 800-171a, SOC2 Type 2, and PCI certifications, with CMMC v2.0 underway, suggest the facility primarily serves federal contractors, defense supply chain entities, and regulated financial services rather than frontier AI labs. These workloads are compute-constrained by security and sovereignty requirements, not by power availability.

For AI scaling, this facility represents the opposite binding constraint from the public cloud hyperscalers. It is not power-limited; it is compliance-constrained. It does not reveal whether Huntsville itself has grid capacity to support additional data center buildout, nor does it address the broader Alabama power supply picture for industrial load.
